title: Gutting, filleting and eating fish
summary: Kill the fish quickly and get it cold. Gut it soon, then fillet it or cook it whole. Keep cleaned fish at 40°F (4°C) or below and cook it within 2 days, or freeze it. Throw out fish that smells sour, rancid or of ammonia. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C). New York’s Department of Health advises how many fish meals a month from which fish; people who could become pregnant (under 50) and children under 15 should eat less of some fish and none of others.

sections.h: Kill it and get it cold

list: Kill the fish quickly (New York Sea Grant), with a blow to the head (Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife). A long, stressful death softens the flesh (Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife).
Bleeding improves the meat of some fish: cut the gill arches with a knife or scissors (Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife, New York Sea Grant).

Get it on ice as soon as it is caught (New York Sea Grant, NYS DEC). An ice slurry cools fish faster: 8 parts ice to 1 part water in a cooler, with ice made from drinking water, topped up with more ice as it melts (New York Sea Grant).
Keeping fish alive until you clean them is in Fishing for food.

blocks.label: Food from the land: where to start

blocks.p: In short: cut from the vent to the gills, pull the guts out. NYS DEC’s field dressing steps:

steps: Make a shallow cut from the vent (the small opening on the belly toward the tail) to the gills. Keep the blade shallow so you don’t cut the stomach or intestines.
Cut the bridge that attaches the gills, and pull out the gills and the guts.
Scrape out the long red kidney along the backbone, with the knife blade or your thumbnail.
Rinse the belly and pack the fish in a cooler with ice.

blocks.cap: The vent is the small opening on the belly toward the tail.

list: Gut a large fish as soon as you catch it and pack the belly with ice. A small fish you will fillet the same day need not be gutted (New York Sea Grant).
If gut contents spill, rinse the belly at once (Maine Department of Inland Fisheries and Wildlife).
Then scale or skin it (US Army). Always cut away from yourself (NYS DEC).

blocks.p: NYS DEC’s steps:

steps: Lay the fish flat on its side. Cut behind the pectoral fin (the side fin behind the gills) down to the backbone, but not through it.
Without taking the knife out, turn the blade and cut toward the tail, through the rib cage, with the blade flat along the backbone (not through it).
Stop just before the fillet comes off. Flip it over, skin side down, still attached.
Slide the knife between the meat and the skin and, holding it almost flat, work it back and forth to take the fillet off the skin.
Carefully cut out the rib cage from the fillet.
Turn the fish over and do the same on the other side. Rinse the fillets in cold, clean water.

blocks.p: Pan dressing, NYS DEC’s steps:

steps: Scrape off the scales on both sides, from the tail toward the head, with a scale scraper or the back of a knife.
Cut 1/4 to 1/2 inch (6 to 12 mm) deep along each side of the back fin and the fin under the belly, so they can come out later.
Hold the fish on its back and cut just behind the vent; slide the knife forward just under the skin to the pectoral fin.
Lay it flat and cut deep on both sides behind the pectoral fin, without cutting the backbone.
Pull the head upward to break the backbone: the head tears loose and the guts and the side and belly fins come with it.
Pull the back and belly fins away and forward (pliers help), cut off the tail, and rinse in cold, clean water.

blocks.p: Boiling fish with the skin on keeps its fat and juices, and the water makes a broth. Fish can also be roasted on a stick, baked or fried (US Army).

list: Cleaned fish keeps up to 2 days in a fridge (NYS DEC). FDA: keep fish you will use within 2 days at 40°F (4°C) or below; otherwise wrap it tightly in plastic, foil or moisture-proof paper and freeze it. Thaw it in the fridge overnight (FDA).
New York Sea Grant says to freeze it if you can’t cook it within two or three days; this app goes by the shorter time, 2 days.
No ice and no cold: fish is perishable food. From Is it still good?, word for word: “never leave perishable food out for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour if it is above 90°F (32°C) (CDC).”

blocks.warn: Don’t eat fish that seems to have gone bad: cooking does not make it safe (US Army). If raw or cooked fish smells sour, rancid or fishy, don’t eat it; seafood gone bad can also smell of ammonia (FDA). Other signs: sunken eyes, faded scales, gills that are not red to pink, flesh that keeps the dent of your thumb, a slimy body, or a sharp or peppery taste (US Army).

blocks.p: From Field dressing game, word for word: “Cook all wild game and birds to at least 165°F in the thickest part, and fish to 145°F.”

list: Most seafood should reach 145°F (63°C) inside (FDA). No thermometer: FDA says, “If you don’t have a food thermometer, there are other ways to determine whether seafood is done.” For fish, its sign is flesh that “separates easily with a fork” (FDA).
Cook all freshwater fish, to kill parasites (US Army).
New York Sea Grant gives 140°F (60°C) for one minute; this app goes by FDA’s higher 145°F (63°C).
Wash your hands for at least 20 seconds after handling raw fish, and clean cutting boards and knives before they touch cooked or ready-to-eat food (FDA).

sections.h: New York’s advice on eating fish you catch

blocks.p: From the NYS Department of Health: its statewide advice was issued in 2024 (page revised March 2025), and its waterbody advice was last updated in April 2026. It applies to waters with no advice of their own, outside the Adirondack and Catskill regions, which have their own regional advice. Some waters have advice of their own (the Central New York ones are in the second table): in April 2026 it was made stricter for Lake Ontario, Lake Erie, the upper Niagara River, part of the Mohawk River, Cumberland Bay of Lake Champlain, Lake George, Seneca Lake and Catharine Creek. In normal times, check the Department’s list for your water before you eat what you catch.

Who: the Department gives one advice for people who may become pregnant (under age 50) and children under 15, and another for everyone else, called “most people” here (NYS Department of Health). A meal in this advice is one-half pound (227 g) of fish; you could eat two quarter-pound meals in place of one (NYS Department of Health). Chemicals in fish can affect unborn babies and children’s development, can stay in the body for decades, and can pass to a baby through breastfeeding (NYS Department of Health).

blocks.p: To lower the chemicals in a meal (NYS Department of Health):

list: Choose smaller fish of a kind: they may carry less.

Remove the skin and trim all the fat from the belly flap, the line along the sides, the back and under the skin. This lowers the chemicals that collect in fat, but not mercury, which is in the meat itself.
Broil, grill or bake the trimmed, skinned fish on a rack so the fat drips away, and don’t use the drippings for sauce or gravy. Cooking or soaking fish cannot get rid of the chemicals.
Spread your meals out: if the advice is up to 4 meals a month, don’t eat them all in one week. This matters most for women and young children.
